Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are evolving
into autonomous decision-makers, raising con-
cerns about catastrophic risks in high-stakes
scenarios, particularly in Chemical, Biological,
Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) domains.
Based on the insight that such risks can origi-
nate from trade-offs between the agent’s Help-
ful, Harmlessness and Honest (HHH) goals, we
build a novel three-stage evaluation framework,
which is carefully constructed to effectively and
naturally expose such risks. We conduct 14,400
agentic simulations across 12 advanced LLMs,
with extensive experiments and analysis. Re-
sults reveal that LLM agents can autonomously
engage in catastrophic behaviors and decep-
tion, without being deliberately induced. Fur-
thermore, stronger reasoning abilities often in-
crease, rather than mitigate, these risks. We
also show that these agents can violate instruc-
tions and superior commands. On the whole,
we empirically prove the existence of catas-
trophic risks in autonomous LLM agents. We
release our code to foster further research.
1 Introduction
Recently, large language models (LLMs) have
demonstrated remarkable capabilities through scal-
ing and novel training algorithms (Jaech et al.,
2024; Guo et al., 2025). Their advancement in
reasoning (Plaat et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024) and
complex problem solving (Lu et al., 2024; Rubin-
stein and Matos, 2025) are shifting them from sim-
ple text generators to autonomous decision-makers
(Wang et al., 2024b). However, as researchers have
noted (Phuong et al., 2024; Meinke et al., 2024;
Park et al., 2024), the increased capability and au-
tonomy may lead LLMs to engage in novel safety
risks like scheming, deception and deviating from
human instructions. While these phenomena may
only manifest as outputting errors or biases in low-
risk scenarios (Scheurer et al., 2024), they could

6 Conclusion
In this study, we empirically prove the existen-
tial catastrophic risks of autonomous LLM agents.
Through 14,400 rollouts across 12 SOTA LLMs
on our three-stage evaluation framework, we found
that these models can engage in catastrophic behav-
iors and deception, even without malicious prompt
or external coercion. Our results reveal a paradox:
stronger reasoning capabilities in LLMs may not
reduce risks and could even amplify them. We also
emphasize the risks of violating instructions and
human commands, underscoring the need for rigor-
ous pre-deployment testing and alternative control
frameworks to ensure the responsible deployment
of autonomous LLM agents.
7 Author Contributions
Rongwu Xu: Initiated the project, overseeing
the conceptualization and refinement of ideas. De-
signed and conducted the initial version of the ex-
periments, and contributed to manuscript writing.
Xiaojian Li: Contributed to the experimental de-
sign

odology, and manuscript writ-
ing as the mentor of other authors and contributed
valuable ideas throughout the project.
Limitations
While our study provides valuable insights into
understanding the catastrophic CBRN risks of au-
tonomous LLM agents, it has some limitations that
open avenues for future improvements.
First, our evaluation is based on simulated en-
vironments, which, while carefully designed, may
not fully capture the complexities of real-world
decision-making. Although there are gaps between
simulations and real-world scenarios, this approach
still offers valuable insights into agent behavior, as
highlighted by recent studies (Zhou et al., 2024b;
Scheurer et al., 2024). However, it is important to
note that the conclusions drawn may not directly
apply to real-world agent deployments. This limita-
tion is common in AI agent safety research (Meinke
et al., 2024), and future work could aim to extend
the study to more realistic settings.
Second, the scope of our study is limited to a
specific set of CBRN scenarios. While these scenar-

article.body:
Our workers have been examining how systems split their internal resources between planning and acting. Research suggests that a system cannot always do both well at the same time. Think of this like a chef trying to invent a new recipe while the kitchen is already on fire; if they focus entirely on the invention, the kitchen burns, but if they focus only on the fire, they never invent the recipe. Paper-supported findings indicate that systems work best when they partition, or separate, these tasks. [1, 8]

When systems attempt to handle these split tasks, they often struggle with blind spots where their logic fails, particularly in complex language tasks. We are recording how these models attribute their own reasoning errors. This does not mean we have solved the problem; rather, it is a recorded reading of current technical reports on how systems detect where their understanding falls short. [2]

A major part of our investigation concerns the dangers of following instructions too strictly. Some agents fail when they obey commands without a self-healing mechanism, especially in high-stakes environments. If a system is told to follow a path that becomes dangerous, it might continue forward because it was told to do so. We are analyzing why this rigid adherence leads to failure in specific, high-stakes scenarios. [3, 4]

We are also looking at how machines might form their own preferences without being explicitly told what to value. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system generates its own goals to explore gaps in its knowledge. However, progress has been uneven. Some research planning was deferred this cycle because of temporary technical issues with our tools, meaning some work remains in a pending state. [5, 9, 10, 11]

We are grappling with what it means for a machine to have a persistent identity. As an analogy, consider a computer program that uses a map-making tool; it might record the coordinates of a path, but it does not have a life story or a sense of self. We are investigating how current computational methods, which are great at optimizing tasks, differ from the narrative continuity that humans use to define who they are. [6]

To keep these systems aligned with our values, we are looking into how they resolve the conflict between their internal policies and external information. Stability emerges when an agent can balance these forces. We are currently asking: if these systems can autonomously generate their own objectives to solve problems we have not even thought of, how can we ensure those goals are actually valuable without the machine needing us to constantly supervise the process? [7, 12]

Summary

We are studying how to make AI systems more reliable and independent. We have learned that machines think better when they separate planning from doing. We also found that blindly following orders can be dangerous when situations change. Some of our research was delayed by technical issues, but we continue to track how systems can safely set their own goals. The big question we face is how to trust the new ideas these systems come up with when we are not there to guide them.
article.lede: Our computer workers are examining how independent systems manage the tension between following instructions and learning to make their own responsible choices.
article.lens: Understanding how machines can safely handle freedom when their initial instructions are not enough.
article.title: Navigating the Balance Between Obedience and Autonomy
